latest_nl_proof:
Let S = S(k). We show that S is a numerical semigroup by verifying that it is a cofinite additive submonoid of N0.

First, 0 belongs to S, because 0 = 0*m + 0 satisfies the defining condition with residue 0.

Second, S is closed under addition. Take x,y in S. Write x = a*m + r and y = b*m + s with a,b >= 0 and 0 <= r,s <= m-1, where if r > 0 then a >= k_r and if s > 0 then b >= k_s. We consider cases.

If r = 0, then x + y = (a+b)*m + s. If s = 0, this is a nonnegative multiple of m and hence lies in S. If s > 0, then b >= k_s, so a+b >= b >= k_s. Therefore (a+b)*m + s lies in S. The case s = 0 is symmetric.

Now assume r,s > 0. Let i = min(r,s) and j = max(r,s). Then 1 <= i <= j <= m-1 and {i,j} = {r,s}. If r+s < m, then x+y = (a+b)*m + (r+s). Since i+j = r+s < m, the Kunz inequality gives k_i + k_j >= k_{r+s}. Hence a+b >= k_r + k_s = k_i + k_j >= k_{r+s}, so x+y lies in S. If r+s = m, then x+y = (a+b+1)*m, which lies in S because every nonnegative multiple of m lies in S. If r+s > m, set t = r+s-m. Then 1 <= t <= m-1 and x+y = (a+b+1)*m + t. Since i+j = r+s > m, the Kunz inequality gives k_i + k_j + 1 >= k_t. Therefore a+b+1 >= k_r + k_s + 1 = k_i + k_j + 1 >= k_t, so x+y lies in S.

Thus S is an additive submonoid of N0.

Third, the complement of S in N0 is finite. By Euclidean division, every n in N0 can be written uniquely as n = q*m + r with q >= 0 and 0 <= r <= m-1. If r = 0 then n lies in S. If r > 0, then by definition n lies in S exactly when q >= k_r. Hence n fails to lie in S exactly when 0 <= q < k_r. Therefore the complement of S in N0 is the finite union, over r = 1,...,m-1, of the finite sets {q*m + r : 0 <= q < k_r}. So S is a numerical semigroup.

Now determine its multiplicity. The element m = 1*m + 0 lies in S. On the other hand, if 0 < n < m, then n = 0*m + n with residue n in {1,...,m-1}; to lie in S it would have to satisfy 0 >= k_n, impossible because k_n is positive. So no positive element of S is smaller than m. Therefore the smallest positive element of S, that is, its multiplicity, is m.

Finally fix r in {1,...,m-1}. A nonnegative integer is congruent to r modulo m exactly when it has the form q*m + r with q >= 0. By the definition of S, such an element lies in S exactly when q >= k_r. The smallest admissible q is therefore q = k_r, and the corresponding element is r + m*k_r. Hence the least element of S congruent to r modulo m is w_r = r + m*k_r.

This proves all claims.
role_in_parent: Provides the inverse construction from an admissible Kunz vector to a numerical semigroup.
statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2, and let k_1,...,k_{m-1} be positive integers satisfying the Kunz inequalities: for all integers i,j with 1 <= i <= j <= m-1, if i + j < m then k_i + k_j >= k_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then k_i + k_j + 1 >= k_{i+j-m}. Define a subset S(k) of N0 by S(k) = {q m + r : q,r are integers, q >= 0, 0 <= r <= m-1, and either r = 0 or q >= k_r}. Then S(k) is a numerical semigroup, its multiplicity is m, and for each r in {1,...,m-1} the least element of S(k) congruent to r modulo m is w_r = r + m k_r.

domain_restrictions: Kunz inequalities quantified over integers i,j with 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ m-1
Case 1 (lower sum): if i + j < m then require k_i + k_j ≥ k_{i+j} (index i+j lies in {1,...,m-1})
Case 2 (upper sum): if i + j > m then require k_i + k_j + 1 ≥ k_{i+j-m} (index i+j-m lies in {1,...,m-1})
Set definition: elements of S(k) are of the form q m + t with q ∈ ℤ, q ≥ 0 and t ∈ ℤ, 0 ≤ t ≤ m-1
Inclusion rule for residue t: (t = 0) OR (t > 0 and q ≥ k_t)
Implicit: k_t is only used for t ∈ {1,...,m-1}; no k_0 is required
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every integer m ≥ 2 and every choice of positive integers k_1,...,k_{m-1} satisfying the Kunz inequalities (for all i,j with 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ m-1: if i+j<m then k_i+k_j ≥ k_{i+j}; if i+j>m then k_i+k_j+1 ≥ k_{i+j-m}), define S(k) = {q m + t : q ∈ ℤ, q ≥ 0, t ∈ {0,1,...,m-1}, and (t=0 or q ≥ k_t)}. Then S(k) is a numerical semigroup whose multiplicity (smallest positive element) equals m, and for each r ∈ {1,...,m-1}, the least element of S(k) congruent to r modulo m is exactly w_r = r + m k_r.
quantifier_order: For all integers m with m ≥ 2
For all families (k_1,...,k_{m-1}) of positive integers satisfying the Kunz inequalities
For all integers i,j with 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ m-1 (subject to conditional cases on i+j relative to m)
For each r ∈ {1,...,m-1} (least element assertion in the congruence class r mod m)
